topics.h: Have you ever searched the whole house for something that was right in front of you? Let's read a funny story about that!
p: A humorous story is a funny story that makes us smile or laugh.
The fun often comes from a surprise, a silly mistake or a mix-up.
Family stories show how family members care for, help and laugh with each other.
While reading, ask: Who is in the story? What happened? Why is it funny?
To answer a question, go back and find the line that gives the answer.

ex.q: Read: Dadi could not find her glasses. She looked under the sofa and behind the TV. She even looked in Bholu the cat's basket. 'Who has hidden my glasses?' she cried. Little Tara giggled and pointed at the fruit bowl. There they were, resting on a mango! Dadi had put them down while choosing fruit. The whole family laughed, and Dadi laughed the loudest. Why did the family laugh?
st: Find where the glasses were: on a mango in the fruit bowl.
Find who put them there: Dadi herself, while choosing fruit.
Think: Dadi blamed someone else, but it was her own mix-up. That surprise is funny.
ex.a: They laughed because Dadi thought someone had hidden her glasses, but she had left them on a mango herself.

topics.rl: In our families, someone is always looking for keys, a phone or the TV remote. These little mix-ups become the funny stories we tell again and again.

topics.h: Your Papa has a brother and your Mummy has a sister. What do you call them in English? Let's learn family words!
p: Family words name our relations: father, mother, brother, sister, grandfather, grandmother.
Your father's or mother's brother is your uncle. Their sister is your aunt.
The children of your uncle or aunt are your cousins.
Your brother's or sister's son is your nephew. Their daughter is your niece.
Masculine words name males (uncle, king). Feminine words name females (aunt, queen). Some words like cousin, friend and child can be used for both.

ex.q: Riya's mother's brother is visiting for Raksha Bandhan. Riya calls him Mama ji. What is the English family word for him?
st: He is the brother of Riya's mother.
A parent's brother is called an uncle in English.
ex.a: Uncle

topics.rl: At weddings and festivals, we meet many relatives. Knowing family words helps us introduce them: 'This is my aunt, and this is my cousin Aarav.'

topics.h: 'Where are my spectacles?' 'Oh no, I sat on them!' Each of these sentences needs a different mark at the end. Can you spot them?
p: A telling sentence (statement) ends with a full stop (.): Papa is reading the newspaper.
An asking sentence (question) ends with a question mark (?): Where are my spectacles?
A sentence that shows strong feeling ends with an exclamation mark (!): What a funny face!
An order or a request usually ends with a full stop: Please pass the chutney.
Every sentence begins with a capital letter. Names of people and places begin with capitals too.

ex.q: Write it correctly: where did chacha keep his spectacles
st: It begins a sentence, so 'where' becomes 'Where'.
'Chacha' is a name, so it gets a capital C.
It asks something, so it ends with a question mark.
ex.a: Where did Chacha keep his spectacles?

topics.rl: Messages to family, notes on the fridge and school homework all need the right capital letters and end marks so the reader understands you.

topics.h: Vroom, vroom... cough, cough... STOP! What happens when a scooter trip does not go as planned? Let's find out!
p: An adventure is an exciting trip or happening, often with a problem to solve.
Adventure stories keep us wondering: What will happen next?
The characters face a problem and find a way to solve it.
Look for clues about how the characters feel: scared, tired, excited, happy.
Safety matters on every ride: riders wear helmets and follow traffic rules.

ex.q: Read: Last Sunday, Chachu took me to the lake on his old red scooter. We both wore our helmets. On the way, the scooter began to cough and splutter. Then it stopped near a sugarcane field! We pushed it along the road for a long time. A kind farmer gave us water and showed us a repair shop. By evening we reached the lake, tired, dusty and very happy. What problem did Chachu and the narrator face, and how was it solved?
st: Find the problem: the scooter coughed, spluttered and stopped near a sugarcane field.
Find the help: a kind farmer gave water and showed them a repair shop.
Put it together: problem, then help, then a happy ending at the lake.
ex.a: The scooter broke down; they pushed it, and a kind farmer showed them a repair shop, so they reached the lake by evening.

topics.rl: Family trips on bikes, buses or trains often have small surprises, like a flat tyre or a late train. Telling them later makes a great adventure story!

topics.t: Telling a story in the past
topics.h: Stories about yesterday need special verbs. 'Today I go' becomes 'Yesterday I went'. Let's learn the past tense!
p: We tell about things that already happened using the simple past tense.
Many verbs just add -ed: push becomes pushed, walk becomes walked.
Some change their spelling: stop becomes stopped, carry becomes carried.
Some verbs change completely: go-went, take-took, ride-rode, see-saw, give-gave, buy-bought.
With 'did' we use the base verb: Did you go? We did not go.

ex.q: Change to the past: 'We ride to the market and buy mangoes.'
st: Find the verbs: ride and buy.
'Ride' changes to 'rode'.
'Buy' changes to 'bought'.
ex.a: We rode to the market and bought mangoes.

topics.rl: When you tell your friends about your holiday or write a diary, you use the past tense: 'I visited Nani. We ate mangoes.'

topics.h: Every story has a storyteller. Sometimes the storyteller is in the story, and sometimes not. Can you tell which?
p: The narrator is the person who tells the story.
In first-person narration, the narrator is part of the story and says I, me, my, we and us.
In third-person narration, the narrator tells about others using he, she, they, his and her.
Sequence words like first, then, next, after that and finally tell the order of events.
A good story has a beginning, a middle and an end.

ex.q: Read: 'I held on tight as the scooter went down the hill.' Is this first-person or third-person narration?
st: Look at who is speaking: the word 'I' is used.
'I' means the narrator is part of the story.
ex.a: First-person narration

topics.rl: When you tell your class 'I went to the zoo', you are a first-person narrator. A news reporter telling about a match is a third-person narrator.

topics.h: A rainbow is like a surprise gift after the rain. Poets love to write about it. Let's read a little rainbow poem!
p: A poem is written in lines. A group of lines is called a stanza.
Rhyming words end with the same sound: new-hue, bright-light, rain-train.
Poets use word pictures (imagery) so we can see, hear and feel what they describe.
Reading a poem aloud helps us enjoy its rhythm, like the beat of a song.
A poet may call one thing by another name, like calling a rainbow 'a painted bridge'.

ex.q: Read the poem: After the rain, the sky is new, / A shining bow of every hue. / Red and orange, yellow bright, / Green and blue in golden light, / Indigo and violet too, / A painted bridge for me and you! Which words rhyme with 'too'?
st: Look at the line that ends with 'too': 'Indigo and violet too'.
Look at the next line's last word: 'you'.
'Too' and 'you' end with the same sound.
ex.a: 'You' rhymes with 'too' (and 'new' and 'hue' have the same sound too).

topics.rl: Songs, nursery rhymes and film songs all use rhyming words. That is why they are so easy to remember!

topics.h: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red. Say VIBGYOR fast three times!
p: A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through raindrops in the air.
Sunlight is made of seven colours. We remember their order as VIBGYOR.
To see a rainbow, stand with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you.
A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as': as green as a parrot; the rainbow is like a bridge.
Word pictures (imagery) help the reader see, hear, smell, taste or feel something.

ex.q: Complete the simile: 'The mango leaves are as green as a ___.' Choose from: parrot, crow, cloud.
st: A simile compares two things that share something.
We need something that is green.
A parrot is green; a crow is black and a rain cloud is grey.
ex.a: as green as a parrot

topics.rl: After a monsoon shower in the evening, look at the sky away from the sun. You may spot a rainbow!

topics.h: The sky is bright. The rainbow is brighter. The sun is the brightest! Let's learn how describing words change.
p: Describing words (adjectives) tell us more about a noun: a colourful rainbow, five birds, a happy child.
To compare two things, we add -er or use 'more': brighter, more beautiful.
To compare more than two things, we add -est or use 'most': brightest, most beautiful.
Spelling changes: big-bigger-biggest, pretty-prettier-prettiest, wide-wider-widest.
Some words change completely: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst.

ex.q: Choose: 'The rainbow is ___ than the grey clouds.' (bright, brighter, brightest)
st: We are comparing two things: the rainbow and the clouds.
For two things we use the -er form.
The word 'than' also tells us to use the -er form.
ex.a: brighter

topics.rl: In shops we hear, 'This one is cheaper,' and in sports, 'She is the fastest runner.' That is comparing!

topics.t: A folk tale of a clever parrot
topics.h: Can a little parrot be wiser than a whole court of ministers? In folk tales, anything can happen!
p: A folk tale is an old story that people told aloud for many years before it was written down.
Folk tales often begin with 'Long ago' or 'Once upon a time'.
They have kings, clever heroes and animals that can talk.
Most folk tales teach a lesson, called a moral.
India has many well-loved tales, such as the Panchatantra, the Jataka tales and stories of Tenali Rama.

ex.q: Read: Long ago, a king had a parrot named Mithu who lived in a silver cage. One day, the king asked his court a riddle: 'What grows bigger the more you share it?' No minister could answer. Mithu called out, 'Happiness, Your Majesty!' The pleased king said, 'Ask for any reward.' Mithu replied, 'Please open my cage and let me fly.' The king kept his word. Now Mithu visits the palace garden every morning as a free friend. Why did Mithu ask for an open cage as his reward?
st: The king offered any reward.
Mithu asked, 'Please open my cage and let me fly.'
He could have asked for anything, but he chose to fly free. Freedom mattered most to him.
ex.a: Because Mithu valued freedom more than any riches.

topics.rl: Grandparents often tell folk tales at bedtime. Many of these stories are hundreds of years old and still teach us about kindness and cleverness.

topics.h: Clever, smart, wise... these words are cousins! Free and caged are opposites. Let's play with word meanings!
p: Synonyms are words with the same or nearly the same meaning: clever and smart; happy and glad.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: wise and foolish; open and shut.
Using synonyms makes our writing more interesting, so we do not repeat the same word.
Antonyms help us show contrast: The cage was shut, but now it is open.
Some words have more than one opposite: free can be the opposite of caged or of costly.

ex.q: In 'The clever parrot asked the king to open the cage', give a synonym of 'clever' and an antonym of 'open'.
st: Clever means quick at thinking. A word with a similar meaning is 'smart'.
The opposite of open is 'shut' or 'close'.
ex.a: Synonym of clever: smart. Antonym of open: shut.

topics.rl: When you write a story, using synonyms like 'shouted, called, cried' instead of 'said' again and again makes it lively.

topics.t: Joining ideas: and, but, because, so, or
topics.h: Mithu was clever. Mithu won his freedom. Can we join these two sentences with one small word? Yes, we can!
p: Joining words (conjunctions) join words or sentences.
'and' adds one idea to another: The king and the queen smiled.
'but' shows a contrast: The cage was pretty, but Mithu wanted to be free.
'because' gives a reason; 'so' gives a result.
'or' gives a choice: Would you like a guava or a chilli?

ex.q: Join with the best word: 'The parrot was clever. It won its freedom.'
st: The first part is the reason; the second part is the result.
'so' joins a reason to its result.
Put a comma before 'so'.
ex.a: The parrot was clever, so it won its freedom.

topics.rl: We use joining words all day: 'I am hungry, so I will eat.' 'Shall we play cricket or kho-kho?'

topics.h: Croak! Splash! Plop! Some words sound just like the noise they name. Let's hear them in a frog poem!
p: Animal poems tell us how an animal looks, moves and sounds.
Sound words copy the sound they name: croak, splash, plop, buzz, hiss.
Rhyming words at the ends of lines make a poem fun to read aloud: grows-toes, fall-all.
Poets choose action words that show movement: hop, leap, kick, dive.
Read the poem twice: once for fun, once to find the answers.

ex.q: Read the poem: Down by the pond where the lotus grows, / Sits a little frog on his tippy toes. / 'Croak!' goes the frog when the raindrops fall, / 'Splash!' goes the frog, the happiest of all. / 'Plop!' in the water, kick, kick, kick, / His long back legs are strong and quick. Which sound words does the poet use?
st: Look for words that copy a sound.
The frog says 'Croak!'
The water sounds are 'Splash!' and 'Plop!'
ex.a: Croak, splash and plop

topics.rl: Comics use sound words all the time: BOOM! ZOOM! SPLASH! In the monsoon, you may hear real frogs croaking near ponds and fields.

topics.h: A frog does not look like a frog when it is a baby! It starts life swimming like a tiny fish. Let's find out how!
p: A frog is an amphibian. It can live both in water and on land.
A frog's life cycle: eggs, then tadpole, then froglet, then adult frog.
Frogs lay their eggs in water. A tadpole lives in water and has a tail.
Most frogs catch insects with a long, sticky tongue.
To describe an animal, tell how it looks, how it moves, what it eats and where it lives.

ex.q: Describe a frog in two sentences, using looks and movement.
st: Looks: a frog has big round eyes, smooth damp skin and long back legs.
Movement: it hops on land and kicks to swim in water.
ex.a: A frog has big round eyes and smooth, damp skin. It hops on land and swims with its strong back legs.

topics.rl: In the monsoon, ponds and puddles near fields fill with tadpoles. Look, but do not touch: frogs have delicate skin.

topics.h: A baby frog is a tadpole. What is a baby cow called? And what do we call a group of bees? Let's find out!
p: Many animals have special names for their young ones: frog-tadpole, cat-kitten, dog-puppy.
More young ones: cow-calf, lion-cub, sheep-lamb, horse-foal, goat-kid, hen-chick, duck-duckling.
A collective noun names a group: a herd of cows, a flock of sheep, a swarm of bees.
More groups: a pride of lions, a school of fish, a troop of monkeys, a bunch of grapes.
We say 'a herd of elephants' because 'herd' names the whole group.

ex.q: Fill in: 'A ___ of bees was buzzing near the hive.'
st: We need a word for a group of bees.
Bees fly together in a swarm.
ex.a: swarm

topics.rl: At a farm you may see a calf, a lamb and a kid. In a forest safari, you might spot a troop of monkeys or a herd of deer!

topics.t: The day the tank went dry
topics.h: Imagine opening the tap to brush your teeth... and nothing comes out! Let's read about a street where that happened.
p: A story has a setting (where and when), characters (who) and a problem.
Look for clue words that tell when: 'one hot May morning', 'at noon', 'that evening'.
Look for the cause of the problem: why did something happen?
Sound words like 'drip, drip, drip' help us hear the story.
A good story often ends with a lesson the characters learn.

ex.q: Read: One hot May morning, the taps in Gully No. 4 went dry. 'The tank on the roof is empty!' shouted Bunty. Everyone went up to the terrace to look. A pipe had been leaking all night, drip, drip, drip. A plumber fixed the pipe, and a water tanker came at noon. That evening, the children made a poster: 'Every drop counts! Close the tap!' Why did the taps go dry?
st: Find the problem: the taps went dry and the tank was empty.
Find the cause: 'A pipe had been leaking all night'.
So the water slowly ran out through the leak.
ex.a: Because a pipe had been leaking all night and the tank became empty.

topics.rl: In many Indian towns, water comes at fixed times and is stored in tanks. A small leak can waste a lot of it, so we must report leaks quickly.

topics.h: 'Close the tap!' 'Fix the leak!' Instructions are short and bossy... but they help save water!
p: An instruction tells someone what to do. It often begins with an action word: Close, Turn, Use, Fix.
To say what not to do, begin with 'Do not' or 'Don't': Don't leave the tap running.
Add 'Please' to make an instruction polite: Please turn off the tap.
Ways to save water: turn off the tap while brushing, use a bucket to bathe, fix leaks, reuse water for plants.
Rainwater harvesting means collecting rainwater and storing it to use later.

ex.q: Change into an instruction: 'You should turn off the tap while brushing your teeth.'
st: An instruction starts with the action word.
Remove 'You should'.
Begin with 'Turn'.
ex.a: Turn off the tap while brushing your teeth.

topics.rl: School posters, recipe steps and game rules are full of instructions. Writing your own 'Save Water' rules for home is a great project!

topics.t: Compound words: two words become one
topics.h: Rain + water = rainwater. Sun + flower = sunflower. Two small words can join to make a brand-new word!
p: A compound word is made by joining two words: rain + coat = raincoat.
The two parts often give a clue to the meaning: a toothbrush is a brush for teeth.
Some compound words have a new meaning: a butterfly is not made of butter!
Water words: rainwater, waterfall, watermelon.
Home words: bathroom, rooftop, teapot, bedroom.

ex.q: Which two words make 'rainwater', and what does it mean?
st: Split the word: rain + water.
Put the meanings together: water that comes from the rain.
ex.a: rain + water: water from the rain

topics.rl: Look around your home: bedroom, toothpaste, cupboard, doorbell. Compound words are everywhere!

topics.t: Gilli danda: a game from long ago
topics.h: No batteries, no screen, just two wooden sticks and a lot of fun! Let's read about gilli danda.
p: Traditional games have been played in India for a very long time.
Gilli danda is played with two pieces of wood: a small gilli with pointed ends and a longer stick called the danda.
Other traditional games are kho-kho, kabaddi, pitthu (lagori) and langdi.
These games need very little equipment and can be played in any open space.
Playing together teaches us teamwork, taking turns and fair play.

ex.q: Read: After school, Irfan and Gopal raced to the open ground with their gilli and danda. The gilli was a small piece of wood with pointed ends. The danda was a longer stick. Gopal tapped one end of the gilli and it flew up. Whack! He hit it far across the ground. Irfan ran and caught it. 'Out!' he laughed. They took turns and played till sunset. Then they walked home together, still laughing. What do you need to play gilli danda?
st: Find the things named: the gilli and the danda.
The gilli is a small piece of wood with pointed ends.
The danda is a longer stick.
ex.a: A small gilli with pointed ends and a longer stick called the danda.

topics.rl: Ask your grandparents which games they played as children. Many will smile and say 'gilli danda' or 'kho-kho'!

topics.t: Action words and how we do them
topics.h: Run! Hit! Catch! Games are full of action words. And HOW do we do them? Quickly, happily, carefully!
p: Verbs are action words: run, hit, catch, throw, jump.
Adverbs tell us more about a verb: how, when or where it happens.
Many adverbs end in -ly: quick-quickly, soft-softly, careful-carefully.
If the word ends in y, change y to i and add -ly: happy-happily, easy-easily.
Some adverbs do not end in -ly: fast, well, hard, soon, here.

ex.q: Find the verb and the adverb: 'Gopal hit the gilli hard.'
st: The action is 'hit', so 'hit' is the verb.
'Hard' tells us how he hit it, so 'hard' is the adverb.
ex.a: Verb: hit. Adverb: hard.

topics.rl: Sports commentators use adverbs all the time: 'She ran swiftly! He bowled cleverly!'

topics.h: Where did the gilli go? Over the wall? Under the bench? Behind the tree? Words of place help us find it!
p: Good friends take turns, share and play fair, whether they win or lose.
Prepositions are words that tell where something is: in, on, under, over, behind, near.
'between' is used for something in the middle of two: The ball is between Irfan and Gopal.
'across' means from one side to the other: He hit the gilli across the ground.
Words in a sentence must be in the right order to make sense.

ex.q: Fill in: 'The gilli flew ___ the wall and landed in the garden next door.'
st: The gilli went up and to the other side of the wall.
A word for going above something to the other side is 'over'.
ex.a: over

topics.rl: When you tell a friend 'Your bat is behind the door' or 'My bottle is in my bag', you use prepositions.

topics.t: A fair decision in the village
topics.h: Two farmers, one calf, and a big quarrel! How can the village find out the truth fairly? Let's read!
p: A panchayat is a group of people who look after the matters of a village.
A fair decision is made after listening to everyone, without taking sides.
A good judge stays calm, asks questions and looks for the truth.
In stories, a clever test can help find out the truth.
Fairness means treating everyone the same way, whether they are rich or poor, friend or stranger.

ex.q: Read: In the village of Rampur, two farmers, Harish and Anil, both said a lost calf was theirs. They went to the panchayat. The Sarpanch listened to both of them calmly. Then she said, 'Let the calf choose.' The calf was set free in the village square. It ran straight to Anil's cow and began to drink milk. 'The calf belongs to Anil,' said the Sarpanch. Harish said sorry, and the two farmers shook hands. Why was letting the calf choose a fair test?
st: A young calf goes to its own mother to drink milk.
Neither farmer could control what the calf did.
So the calf's choice showed the truth, without taking sides.
ex.a: Because the calf would run to its own mother, and nobody could cheat.

topics.rl: In class, when two friends both want the same seat, a fair teacher listens to both before deciding. That is what a good panchayat does too.

topics.t: Words of fairness and their opposites
topics.h: Fair or unfair? Honest or dishonest? Just add a little word-part in front, and the meaning flips!
p: A gram panchayat looks after a village: roads, clean water, drains and more.
The head of a gram panchayat is called the Sarpanch. The members are chosen by the villagers by voting.
Words about fairness: fair, honest, truth, justice, decision, witness.
A prefix is a word-part added to the beginning of a word. un-, dis- and in- can make opposites.
fair-unfair, kind-unkind, honest-dishonest, agree-disagree, justice-injustice, correct-incorrect.

ex.q: Make the opposite with a prefix: 'It was a fair decision.'
st: The word to change is 'fair'.
The prefix 'un-' makes the opposite of 'fair'.
un + fair = unfair.
ex.a: It was an unfair decision.

topics.rl: When we play, we often say 'That's unfair!' Now you know that 'un-' is the part that flips 'fair' into its opposite.

topics.h: "Let the calf choose," said the Sarpanch. See those little marks? They hold the exact words someone said!
p: Speech marks (inverted commas) go around the exact words a person says.
The spoken words begin with a capital letter: The Sarpanch said, "Let the calf choose."
A comma usually comes after 'said' or 'asked' when it comes before the spoken words.
The full stop, question mark or exclamation mark goes inside the closing speech marks.
Use 'asked' for a question, 'replied' for an answer and 'shouted' for loud words.

ex.q: Punctuate: the sarpanch said let the calf choose
st: Begin the sentence with a capital: The Sarpanch.
Put a comma after 'said'.
Put speech marks around her words and begin them with a capital L.
Put the full stop inside the closing speech marks.
ex.a: The Sarpanch said, "Let the calf choose."

topics.rl: Comics show speech in bubbles. In stories and newspapers, speech marks do the same job.

topics.t: A poem about the work people do
topics.h: The baker, the painter, the farmer, the postman... Every day we see people doing different work. Which would you like to do?
p: Poems about work show us the many jobs people do around us.
A vocation is the work a person chooses or feels they are meant to do.
Children often dream about what they will be when they grow up.
Each pair of lines in this poem rhymes: bread-shed, wheat-street, tall-all.
Every kind of honest work is useful and deserves respect.

ex.q: Read the poem: I watch the baker knead the bread, / I watch the painter paint the shed. / The farmer sows the seeds of wheat, / The postman cycles down our street. / I wonder, when I'm grown and tall, / Which one I'll be, or maybe all! What does the child in the poem wonder about?
st: Look at the last two lines.
'I wonder, when I'm grown and tall, / Which one I'll be, or maybe all!'
So the child wonders which work they will do when they grow up.
ex.a: Which of these jobs they will do when they grow up, or maybe all of them!

topics.rl: Think of the people who help your family every day: the vegetable seller, the bus driver, the doctor, the teacher. Each has a vocation.

topics.h: A person who teaches is a teacher. A person who sails is a sailor. Can you guess what a person who paints is called?
p: An occupation is the work a person does to earn a living.
Many worker words are made by adding -er: teach-teacher, farm-farmer, bake-baker.
Some add -or: act-actor, sail-sailor, direct-director.
Some end in -ist or -ian: art-artist, violin-violinist, music-musician, science-scientist.
Some worker words are special: a cobbler mends shoes, a carpenter works with wood.

ex.q: What do we call a person who paints, and how is the word made?
st: Start with the action word: paint.
Add the ending -er.
paint + er = painter.
ex.a: painter

topics.rl: On Career Day at school, children dress up as doctors, pilots, scientists and chefs. Each worker word tells what the person does!

topics.h: 'When I grow up, I will...' Finish that sentence! Today we learn how to talk about the future.
p: We use 'will' + the base verb to talk about the future: I will become a doctor.
'will not' can be shortened to 'won't': I won't give up.
'going to' shows a plan: I am going to learn the tabla.
We can share dreams with 'want to' or 'would like to': I want to be a pilot.
Every dream needs effort today: practise, read and keep asking questions.

ex.q: Change to the future: 'Asha paints a picture.'
st: To talk about the future, use 'will'.
After 'will', use the base verb: paint, not paints.
ex.a: Asha will paint a picture.

topics.rl: On New Year's Day, many people say what they will do in the coming year. These are plans for the future!

topics.h: Clink, clink! Glass bangles shine at weddings and festivals. But how does hard glass become a round, sparkly bangle?
p: Firozabad, a city in Uttar Pradesh, is famous for its glass bangles.
Glass is melted in a very hot furnace until it becomes soft.
The soft glass is shaped into coils, cut into rings and joined with heat.
Then the bangles are polished, painted or decorated.
Many skilled people work on each bangle, step by step.

ex.q: Read: Zoya's family makes glass bangles in Firozabad. Glass is melted in a very hot furnace, so Zoya watches from a safe distance. Her uncle shapes the soft, glowing glass into long coils. The coils are cut into rings, and the ends of each ring are joined with a small flame. Then Zoya's mother paints tiny flowers on them. 'Each bangle carries the work of many hands,' she says proudly. What happens to the glass after it is shaped into coils?
st: Find the line about coils: 'The coils are cut into rings'.
Then: 'the ends of each ring are joined with a small flame'.
ex.a: The coils are cut into rings, and the ends of each ring are joined with a small flame.

topics.rl: When you see a box of shiny bangles at a fair, remember: many artisans worked with great care and skill to make them.

topics.h: A potter turns mud into pots. A weaver turns thread into cloth. Artisans have magic in their hands!
p: An artisan is a skilled worker who makes things by hand.
A potter makes pots from clay. A weaver makes cloth. A carpenter works with wood.
A blacksmith makes tools from iron. A goldsmith makes jewellery from gold.
India has many famous crafts: Madhubani paintings from Bihar, wooden toys from Channapatna in Karnataka, blue pottery from Jaipur.
Handmade things take skill, time and patience, so we should value them.

ex.q: Fill in: 'A ___ shapes wet clay on a wheel to make diyas and pots.'
st: Think: who works with clay?
A person who makes pots is a potter.
ex.a: potter

topics.rl: At Diwali, we light clay diyas made by potters. At a crafts fair, you may see weavers, painters and toy makers at work.

topics.h: One bangle, two bangles... one box, two boxes... one child, many children! Let's learn how words change from one to many.
p: Most nouns add -s to show more than one: bangle-bangles, toy-toys.
Words ending in s, ss, sh, ch or x add -es: bus-buses, glass-glasses, brush-brushes, box-boxes.
Words ending in a consonant + y change y to i and add -es: city-cities, baby-babies.
Many words ending in f or fe change to -ves: knife-knives, leaf-leaves.
Some words change completely or not at all: child-children, woman-women, tooth-teeth, sheep-sheep.

ex.q: Make plural: 'The artisan painted one glass and one box.' Change to many.
st: 'Glass' ends in ss, so add -es: glasses.
'Box' ends in x, so add -es: boxes.
ex.a: The artisan painted many glasses and many boxes.

topics.rl: At the bangle shop: 'Two dozen bangles, please, in two boxes!' We use plurals every time we shop.

qa.q: Read: 'Dadi could not find her glasses. She looked under the sofa and behind the TV. She even looked in Bholu the cat's basket.' Which place did Dadi NOT search?
qa.e: The passage names the sofa, the TV and the cat's basket. It never says she looked inside the cupboard.

qa.q: Read: ''Who has hidden my glasses?' Dadi cried.' What did Dadi think had happened?
qa.e: Her question 'Who has hidden my glasses?' shows she thought someone had hidden them.

qa.q: Read: 'Little Tara giggled and pointed at the fruit bowl. There they were, resting on a mango!' Where were the glasses?
qa.a: On a mango in the fruit bowl
qa.e: The lines say the glasses were resting on a mango in the fruit bowl.

qa.q: Read: 'Dadi had put them down while choosing fruit.' Who had put the glasses on the mango?
qa.e: The line clearly says Dadi had put them down while choosing fruit.

qa.q: What makes Dadi's story funny?
qa.a: She blamed others, but she had left the glasses there herself
qa.e: The surprise is that the 'missing' glasses were left by Dadi herself. A mix-up like this is what makes the story humorous.

qa.q: Read: 'Little Tara giggled.' What does 'giggled' mean?
qa.a: Laughed in a light, silly way
qa.e: To giggle is to laugh lightly, often in a silly or nervous way.

qa.q: Read: 'The whole family laughed, and Dadi laughed the loudest.' What does this tell us about Dadi?
qa.a: She could laugh at her own mistake
qa.e: Laughing the loudest shows Dadi enjoyed the joke, even though the mistake was her own.

qa.q: Which of these is most likely to be part of a humorous story?
qa.a: A funny mix-up that makes readers laugh
qa.e: Humorous stories are written to amuse us, often through mix-ups and surprises.

qa.q: What is the feminine of 'nephew'?
qa.e: A nephew is a brother's or sister's son. A daughter in the same place is a niece.

qa.q: What is the masculine of 'aunt'?
qa.e: Aunt and uncle are a pair: aunt is feminine, uncle is masculine.

qa.q: Your father's father is your ___.
qa.e: The father of your parent is your grandfather.

qa.q: Your aunt's daughter is your ___.
qa.e: The children of your aunts and uncles are your cousins.

qa.q: Which word can be used for both a boy and a girl?
qa.e: A cousin can be a boy or a girl. Brother and king are masculine; niece is feminine.

qa.q: What is the feminine of 'king'?
qa.e: King and queen are a masculine-feminine pair. Princess is the feminine of prince.

qa.q: Meera's brother has a son. What is the son to Meera?
qa.e: A brother's or sister's son is your nephew.

qa.q: What is the masculine of 'lioness'?
qa.e: We add '-ess' to lion to make lioness. So the masculine is lion.

qa.q: Which mark should end this sentence: 'Where is my tiffin box'
qa.e: The sentence asks something, so it ends with a question mark.

qa.q: Which sentence shows strong feeling?
qa.e: 'What a funny joke!' shows surprise and joy, and it ends with an exclamation mark.

qa.q: In 'my cousin lives in jaipur.', which words need capital letters?
qa.e: 'My' is the first word of the sentence, and 'Jaipur' is the name of a place. Both need capitals: My cousin lives in Jaipur.

qa.q: What kind of sentence is 'Please close the door.'?
qa.e: It asks someone politely to do something, so it is a request. It ends with a full stop.

qa.q: Papa cannot read without his spectacles. What are spectacles?
qa.e: Spectacles is another word for glasses that help people see clearly.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'Papa wears a pair of ___.'
qa.e: We say 'a pair of spectacles', just like 'a pair of scissors'. The word is used in the plural.

qa.q: A full stop at the end of a sentence usually shows that the sentence ___.
qa.e: Telling sentences, and also orders and requests, end with a full stop.

qa.q: Which of these needs a question mark?
qa.e: 'Who ate the last laddoo' asks something, so it needs a question mark.

qa.q: Read: 'Last Sunday, Chachu took me to the lake on his old red scooter.' Who took the narrator to the lake?
qa.e: The line says Chachu took the narrator to the lake.

qa.q: Read: 'Then it stopped near a sugarcane field!' Where did the scooter stop?
qa.e: The line says it stopped near a sugarcane field.

qa.q: Read: 'A kind farmer gave us water and showed us a repair shop.' How did the farmer help?
qa.a: He gave water and showed them a repair shop
qa.e: The farmer gave water and showed them where the repair shop was.

qa.q: Read: 'The scooter began to cough and splutter.' What does this tell us?
qa.a: Something was going wrong with the scooter
qa.e: A scooter cannot really cough. These sound words show the engine was having trouble.

qa.q: Read: 'By evening we reached the lake, tired, dusty and very happy.' How did they feel at the end?
qa.e: The line says they were tired, dusty and very happy.

qa.q: Read: 'We both wore our helmets.' Why do riders wear helmets?
qa.e: A helmet protects the head if the rider falls. It is a safety rule for everyone on a two-wheeler.

qa.q: Read: 'A kind farmer gave us water.' Which word describes the farmer?
qa.e: 'Kind' tells us what the farmer was like. It is a describing word.

qa.q: Which of these makes a story an adventure?
qa.a: An exciting journey with a problem to solve
qa.e: Adventure stories have exciting events and problems that the characters must solve.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'go'?
qa.e: 'Go' is an irregular verb. Its simple past is 'went'.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'stop'?
qa.e: For short words like 'stop', we double the last letter before adding -ed: stopped.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'carry'?
qa.e: When a word ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -ed: carried.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'Yesterday, the mechanic ___ Chachu's scooter.'
qa.e: 'Yesterday' tells us it happened in the past, so we use 'fixed'.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'Did you ___ the lake?'
qa.e: After 'did', we use the base form of the verb: see.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'buy'?
qa.e: Buy changes to 'bought'. 'Brought' is the past of 'bring', a different verb.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'catch'?
qa.e: 'Catch' is irregular. Its past is 'caught'.

qa.q: Which sentence is in the past tense?
qa.a: We pushed the scooter to the shop.
qa.e: 'Pushed' ends in -ed and shows the action is over.

qa.q: Read: 'I held on tight as the scooter went down the hill.' Who is telling this?
qa.a: A narrator who is in the story
qa.e: The word 'I' shows the narrator is part of the story. This is first-person narration.

qa.q: Which sentence is written in the third person?
qa.a: She parked the scooter near the gate.
qa.e: 'She' tells about someone else, so it is third person.

qa.q: Which sequence word shows the last event?
qa.e: 'Finally' tells us this is the last thing that happened.

qa.q: Choose the missing word: 'First, we wore helmets. ___, Chachu started the scooter. Finally, we rode away.'
qa.e: The middle step needs a word like 'then'. 'Finally' and 'In the end' are for the last step.

qa.q: The person who tells a story is called the ___.
qa.e: The narrator tells the story. It can be a character or someone outside the story.

qa.q: Which word shows first-person narration?
qa.e: 'We' includes the narrator, so it shows first-person narration.

qa.q: Rohan wrote: 'Rohan and his father went to Ooty.' How would he say it in the first person?
qa.a: My father and I went to Ooty.
qa.e: In the first person, Rohan talks about himself as 'I' and 'my'.

qa.q: What is the right order for the parts of a story?
qa.e: A story starts with a beginning, moves through the middle and finishes with an end.

qa.q: Read: 'Red and orange, yellow bright, / Green and blue in golden light.' Which word rhymes with 'bright'?
qa.e: 'Bright' and 'light' both end with the same '-ight' sound.

qa.q: Read: 'After the rain, the sky is new.' When does the rainbow appear in the poem?
qa.e: The first line says 'After the rain'.

qa.q: Read: 'A shining bow of every hue.' Why does the poet call the rainbow a 'bow'?
qa.a: Because it is curved like a bow
qa.e: An archer's bow is curved. The rainbow has the same curved shape.

qa.q: Read: 'A shining bow of every hue.' What does 'hue' mean?
qa.e: Hue is another word for colour. 'Every hue' means every colour.

qa.q: Read: 'Red and orange, yellow bright, / Green and blue in golden light, / Indigo and violet too.' How many rainbow colours are named?
qa.e: It names red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet: 7 colours. 'Golden' describes the light, not a rainbow colour.

qa.q: Which pair of words rhymes?
qa.e: 'Rain' and 'train' end with the same '-ain' sound.

qa.q: What is a group of lines in a poem called?
qa.e: Poems are made of stanzas. Stories are made of paragraphs.

qa.q: Read: 'A shining bow of every hue.' Which word tells us the rainbow is bright?
qa.e: 'Shining' describes how bright the rainbow looks.

qa.q: In VIBGYOR, what colour does the letter V stand for?
qa.e: VIBGYOR starts with violet. Note the spelling: v-i-o-l-e-t.

qa.q: In VIBGYOR, which colour comes between green and orange?
qa.e: V-I-B-G-Y-O-R: after G (green) comes Y (yellow), then O (orange).

qa.q: When can we see a rainbow?
qa.e: A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through tiny drops of water in the air.

qa.q: Where should the sun be when you look at a rainbow?
qa.e: We see a rainbow when the sun is behind us and the raindrops are in front of us.

qa.q: Which sentence is a simile?
qa.a: Her smile was as bright as the sun.
qa.e: It compares her smile with the sun using 'as ... as'.

qa.q: Complete the simile: 'as black as ___'
qa.e: Coal is black, so 'as black as coal' makes sense. Milk, snow and cotton are white.

qa.q: On the outside edge of a rainbow, which colour do we usually see?
qa.e: In a rainbow, red is on the outer edge and violet is on the inner edge.

qa.q: Which sentence paints the best word picture?
qa.a: Peacocks danced in the silver rain.
qa.e: 'Peacocks danced in the silver rain' helps us see colours and movement. That is imagery.

qa.q: Which word is an adjective in: 'A colourful rainbow appeared.'?
qa.e: 'Colourful' describes the rainbow, so it is an adjective.

qa.q: What is the comparative form of 'big'?
qa.e: Double the 'g' and add -er: bigger. 'Biggest' is the superlative.

qa.q: What is the superlative form of 'good'?
qa.e: Good changes completely: good, better, best.

qa.q: Choose: 'Today is the ___ day of the year.' (hot)
qa.e: We compare one day with all the days of the year, so we use the superlative: hottest.

qa.q: Choose: 'The sky looks ___ than yesterday.' (clear)
qa.e: Two things are compared and the word 'than' is used, so we need 'clearer'.

qa.q: What is the superlative form of 'beautiful'?
qa.e: Long words use 'most' for the superlative: most beautiful.

qa.q: What is the comparative form of 'pretty'?
qa.e: Change y to i and add -er: prettier.

qa.q: Which comparing sentence is correct?
qa.a: An elephant is heavier than a goat.
qa.e: 'Heavier' is the right comparative, and it goes with 'than'.

qa.q: Read: 'A king had a parrot named Mithu who lived in a silver cage.' Where did Mithu live?
qa.e: The line says Mithu lived in a silver cage.

qa.q: Read: ''What grows bigger the more you share it?' ... Mithu called out, 'Happiness, Your Majesty!'' What was Mithu's answer to the riddle?
qa.e: Mithu said happiness grows bigger when you share it.

qa.q: Read: 'No minister could answer. Mithu called out, 'Happiness, Your Majesty!' The pleased king said, 'Ask for any reward.'' Why was the king pleased?
qa.a: Mithu answered the riddle that nobody else could
qa.e: The ministers failed, but Mithu gave a clever answer.

qa.q: Read: 'Mithu replied, 'Please open my cage and let me fly.'' What reward did Mithu ask for?
qa.e: Mithu asked for the cage to be opened so he could fly free.

qa.q: Read: 'The king kept his word.' What does 'kept his word' mean?
qa.a: He did what he had promised
qa.e: To keep your word means to do what you promised. The king promised any reward.

qa.q: What does the tale show about Mithu?
qa.a: He was clever and loved freedom
qa.e: He solved the riddle (clever) and chose to be free (loved freedom).

qa.q: Which lesson does Mithu's tale teach?
qa.a: Freedom is more precious than a silver cage
qa.e: Mithu chose an open sky over a silver cage. That is the moral.

qa.q: What is a folk tale?
qa.a: An old story passed on by people telling it
qa.e: Folk tales are old stories that were told aloud from one person to another, often for many years.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'clever'?
qa.e: Clever and smart both mean quick at thinking and understanding.

qa.q: Which word is an antonym of 'wise'?
qa.e: Wise means having good sense; foolish means having poor sense.

qa.q: Mithu lived in a cage but now flies in the open sky. Which word is the opposite of 'caged'?
qa.e: A caged bird cannot fly away; a free bird can.

qa.q: Which word means nearly the same as 'reward'?
qa.e: A reward is something given for doing well, like a prize.

qa.q: Which word is an antonym of 'brave'?
qa.e: Brave means not afraid; cowardly means easily afraid.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'happy'?
qa.e: Happy and glad mean nearly the same thing.

qa.q: Read: 'The parrot longed to fly over the hills.' What does 'longed' mean?
qa.e: To long for something is to wish for it very much.

qa.q: Which pair of words are antonyms?
qa.e: Open and shut are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.

qa.q: Choose: 'The riddle was hard, ___ nobody could answer it.'
qa.e: The hard riddle (reason) led to nobody answering (result), so we use 'so'.

qa.q: Choose: 'The cage was beautiful, ___ Mithu wanted to be free.'
qa.e: The two ideas are in contrast: a beautiful cage, yet a wish for freedom. 'But' shows contrast.

qa.q: Choose: 'Mithu was happy ___ he was free at last.'
qa.e: The second part gives the reason why Mithu was happy, so we use 'because'.

qa.q: Choose: 'Would you like a guava ___ a chilli, Mithu?'
qa.e: This is a choice between two things, so we use 'or'.

qa.q: Choose: 'The king ___ the queen laughed at the joke.'
qa.e: Both of them laughed. 'And' adds one person to the other.

qa.q: Which word is the joining word in: 'I wanted to play, but it was raining.'?
qa.e: 'But' joins the two parts of the sentence.

qa.q: Which joining word gives a reason?
qa.e: 'Because' tells us why something happened.

qa.q: Which is the best way to join: 'Mithu flew away. He came back every morning.'?
qa.a: Mithu flew away, but he came back every morning.
qa.e: Flying away and coming back are a contrast, so 'but' fits best.

qa.q: Read: 'Down by the pond where the lotus grows, / Sits a little frog on his tippy toes.' Where does the frog sit?
qa.a: By a pond where the lotus grows
qa.e: The first line tells us the frog is down by the pond where the lotus grows.

qa.q: Read: ''Croak!' goes the frog when the raindrops fall.' What does the frog say when it rains?
qa.e: The line says 'Croak!' goes the frog. 'Splash' is the sound of the water.

qa.q: Read: ''Croak!' goes the frog when the raindrops fall, / 'Splash!' goes the frog, the happiest of all.' Which word rhymes with 'fall'?
qa.e: 'Fall' and 'all' end with the same sound.

qa.q: Read: ''Plop!' in the water, kick, kick, kick, / His long back legs are strong and quick.' What helps the frog swim?
qa.e: The poem says his long back legs are strong and quick as he kicks in the water.

qa.q: Which of these is a sound word?
qa.e: 'Splash' copies the sound of water. The others are not sound words.

qa.q: Read: ''Splash!' goes the frog, the happiest of all.' This happens when the raindrops fall. What does it show?
qa.e: Being 'the happiest of all' in the rain shows the frog loves wet weather.

qa.q: Read: 'Sits a little frog on his tippy toes.' What does 'on his tippy toes' mean?
qa.a: On the tips of his toes
qa.e: Tippy toes means standing up on the tips of your toes.

qa.q: Which sound word goes with a bee?
qa.e: Bees make a buzzing sound. Croak is for frogs, moo for cows, neigh for horses.

qa.q: A frog is an amphibian. What does this mean?
qa.a: It can live both in water and on land
qa.e: Amphibians, like frogs, spend part of their life in water and part on land.

qa.q: What is the young frog that hatches from an egg called?
qa.e: A frog egg hatches into a tadpole. A froglet comes later, after the legs have grown.

qa.q: In a frog's life cycle, what comes right after the eggs?
qa.e: Eggs hatch into tadpoles. Tadpoles later become froglets and then adult frogs.

qa.q: How do most frogs catch insects?
qa.e: A frog flicks out its long, sticky tongue to catch insects.

qa.q: Where do frogs lay their eggs?
qa.e: Frogs lay their eggs in water, such as ponds and puddles.

qa.q: Which sentence tells how a frog moves?
qa.e: 'Hops and leaps' are action words that show movement.

qa.q: Which words best describe the skin of most frogs?
qa.e: Most frogs have smooth, damp skin. Fur and feathers belong to other animals.

qa.q: You are describing a frog. Which detail tells where it lives?
qa.e: 'It lives near ponds' tells us its home.

qa.q: What is the young one of a lion called?
qa.e: A baby lion is a cub. Tiger and bear babies are also cubs.

qa.q: What is the young one of a goat called?
qa.e: A baby goat is called a kid. A baby sheep is a lamb.

qa.q: What is the young one of a horse called?
qa.e: A baby horse is a foal.

qa.q: What is the young one of a hen called?
qa.e: A hen's baby is a chick.

qa.q: Choose: 'A ___ of elephants walked to the river.'
qa.e: Large animals like elephants and cows move in a herd.

qa.q: Choose: 'A ___ of birds flew over the fields.'
qa.e: Birds fly together in a flock.

qa.q: Which is a collective noun?
qa.e: 'Swarm' names a group of bees, so it is a collective noun.

qa.q: Choose: 'We saw a ___ of fish in the aquarium.'
qa.e: A group of fish swimming together is called a school.

qa.q: Read: 'One hot May morning, the taps in Gully No. 4 went dry.' When did the taps go dry?
qa.e: The line says 'One hot May morning'.

qa.q: Read: 'A pipe had been leaking all night, drip, drip, drip.' Why was the tank empty?
qa.a: A pipe had been leaking all night
qa.e: The leak let the water drip out all night until the tank was empty.

qa.q: Read: 'A plumber fixed the pipe, and a water tanker came at noon.' Who fixed the pipe?
qa.e: The line clearly says a plumber fixed the pipe.

qa.q: Read: 'A plumber fixed the pipe, and a water tanker came at noon.' When did the water tanker come?
qa.e: Noon means twelve o'clock in the daytime.

qa.q: Read: 'A pipe had been leaking all night, drip, drip, drip.' What do the words 'drip, drip, drip' tell us?
qa.a: Water was falling drop by drop
qa.e: 'Drip' is the sound of single drops falling, again and again.

qa.q: Read: 'The children made a poster: 'Every drop counts! Close the tap!'' What was the poster about?
qa.e: 'Every drop counts' and 'Close the tap' are about saving water.

qa.q: What does 'Every drop counts' mean?
qa.a: Even a little water is important
qa.e: It means even small amounts of water matter, so we should not waste any.

qa.q: Read: ''The tank on the roof is empty!' shouted Bunty.' Where was the water tank?
qa.e: Bunty says 'The tank on the roof'.

qa.q: Which sentence is an instruction?
qa.e: It tells someone what to do and begins with an action word.

qa.q: Which is a good tip for saving water?
qa.a: Use a bucket and mug to bathe.
qa.e: A bucket helps us use only the water we need.

qa.q: Most instructions begin with ___.
qa.e: Instructions usually start with a verb like close, use or fix.

qa.q: Which instruction tells what NOT to do?
qa.e: 'Don't' tells someone not to do something.

qa.q: What is rainwater harvesting?
qa.a: Collecting and storing rainwater to use later
qa.e: We collect rainwater from roofs and store it in tanks or let it soak into the ground.

qa.q: Ammi washed the vegetables in a bowl. What is the best use of that leftover water?
qa.e: Reusing clean leftover water for plants saves fresh water.

qa.q: Which instruction is the most polite?
qa.e: 'Please' makes an instruction polite.

qa.q: Which habit does NOT save water?
qa.a: Washing a car with a running pipe
qa.e: A running pipe wastes a lot of water. A bucket uses much less.

qa.q: Which is a compound word?
qa.e: Toothbrush is made of two words: tooth + brush.

qa.q: sun + light = ?
qa.e: Joining sun and light gives sunlight.

qa.q: Which two words make 'bathroom'?
qa.e: 'Bathroom' is a room for taking a bath: bath + room.

qa.q: Which word can join 'foot' to make a compound word?
qa.e: Foot + ball = football.

qa.q: What is a 'waterfall'?
qa.e: A waterfall is water flowing down from a high place, like a cliff.

qa.q: Which is NOT a compound word?
qa.e: 'Bucket' cannot be split into two words. The others can: roof + top, tea + pot, sun + flower.

qa.q: roof + top = ?
qa.e: Joining roof and top gives rooftop, the top of a roof.

qa.q: A pot for making tea is a ___.
qa.e: Tea + pot = teapot.

qa.q: Read: 'The gilli was a small piece of wood with pointed ends.' What does the gilli look like?
qa.a: A small piece of wood with pointed ends
qa.e: The line describes the gilli as small, wooden and pointed at the ends.

qa.q: Read: 'The danda was a longer stick.' What is the danda?
qa.e: The danda is the longer stick used to hit the gilli.

qa.q: Read: 'Gopal tapped one end of the gilli and it flew up. Whack! He hit it far across the ground.' What did Gopal do first?
qa.a: He tapped one end of the gilli
qa.e: First he tapped the gilli to make it fly up. Then he hit it.

qa.q: Read: 'Irfan ran and caught it. 'Out!' he laughed.' Who said 'Out!'?
qa.e: Irfan caught the gilli and laughed, 'Out!'

qa.q: Read: 'Whack! He hit it far across the ground.' What kind of word is 'Whack'?
qa.e: 'Whack' copies the sound of a stick hitting something.

qa.q: Read: 'They took turns and played till sunset. Then they walked home together, still laughing.' What do these lines show about the boys?
qa.a: They were good friends who played fairly
qa.e: Taking turns and laughing together shows friendship and fair play.

qa.q: Which of these is a traditional Indian game?
qa.e: Kho-kho has been played in Indian villages and schools for a long time.

qa.q: Why can gilli danda be played almost anywhere there is open space?
qa.a: It needs only two wooden sticks
qa.e: Gilli danda needs very little: a gilli and a danda.

qa.q: Which word is the verb in: 'Irfan caught the gilli.'?
qa.e: 'Caught' is the action.

qa.q: Which word is the adverb in: 'Gopal ran quickly to the ground.'?
qa.e: 'Quickly' tells us how Gopal ran.

qa.q: Change 'happy' into an adverb.
qa.e: Change y to i and add -ly: happily.

qa.q: Choose: 'The children played ___ in the park.'
qa.e: We need a word that tells how they played, so we use the adverb 'happily'.

qa.q: Which is an action word?
qa.e: 'Throw' is something you do. The others are describing or naming words.

qa.q: Read: 'Meena plays kabaddi well.' What does 'well' tell us?
qa.e: 'Well' is an adverb that tells how she plays.

qa.q: Change 'careful' into an adverb.
qa.e: Just add -ly: careful + ly = carefully, with two l's.

qa.q: Choose: 'The friends cheered ___ when Gopal hit the gilli far.'
qa.e: We need an adverb to tell how they cheered: loudly.

qa.q: Choose: 'We ran ___ the ground to reach the other side.'
qa.e: 'Across' means from one side to the other.

qa.q: Choose: 'Rani is sitting ___ Meena and Joseph.'
qa.e: We use 'between' for someone in the middle of two people.

qa.q: Which word is a preposition in: 'The danda is near the door.'?
qa.e: 'Near' tells us where the danda is.

qa.q: Choose: 'Gopal hid ___ the tree, so Irfan could not see him.'
qa.e: If Gopal is behind the tree, the tree blocks Irfan's view.

qa.q: Choose: 'Put your shoes ___ the shelf.'
qa.e: Things rest on a shelf.

qa.q: Which shows fair play in a game?
qa.e: Fair play means giving everyone a turn and following the rules.

qa.q: Your friend loses the game and looks sad. What is the kind thing to say?
qa.a: Well played! Let's play again tomorrow.
qa.e: Good friends cheer each other up, whether they win or lose.

qa.q: Which sentence has the words in the right order?
qa.e: An English sentence usually goes: who (Gopal), action (hit), what (the gilli), then more (far).

qa.q: Read: 'Harish and Anil both said a lost calf was theirs. They went to the panchayat.' Why did the farmers go to the panchayat?
qa.a: Both said the calf was theirs
qa.e: Both farmers claimed the same calf, so they needed a fair decision.

qa.q: Read: 'The Sarpanch listened to both of them calmly.' How did the Sarpanch listen?
qa.e: She listened to both, and she stayed calm. That is fair.

qa.q: Read: 'Then she said, 'Let the calf choose.'' What was the Sarpanch's idea?
qa.e: Her plan was to let the calf show whose it was.

qa.q: Read: 'It ran straight to Anil's cow and began to drink milk.' What did the calf do?
qa.a: It ran to Anil's cow and drank milk
qa.e: The calf went straight to its mother, Anil's cow.

qa.q: Read: 'Harish said sorry, and the two farmers shook hands.' How did the quarrel end?
qa.a: Peacefully, with the farmers shaking hands
qa.e: Saying sorry and shaking hands shows the quarrel ended in peace.

qa.q: Read: 'The Sarpanch listened to both of them calmly.' What does 'calmly' mean?
qa.e: Calm means peaceful and not upset. 'Calmly' is how she listened.

qa.q: What makes a decision fair?
qa.a: Listening to everyone and not taking sides
qa.e: A fair judge hears all sides and looks for the truth.

qa.q: Read: 'The calf belongs to Anil,' said the Sarpanch. Who is the Sarpanch?
qa.a: The head of the village panchayat
qa.e: The Sarpanch is the head of the gram panchayat.

qa.q: What is the head of a gram panchayat called?
qa.e: The Sarpanch leads the gram panchayat.

qa.q: How are the members of a gram panchayat chosen?
qa.e: Panchayat members are elected: the villagers vote to choose them.

qa.q: Which is the opposite of 'fair'?
qa.e: We add 'un-' to fair to make 'unfair'.

qa.q: Which is the opposite of 'honest'?
qa.e: We add 'dis-' to honest to make 'dishonest'.

qa.q: Which is the opposite of 'justice'?
qa.e: We add 'in-' to justice to make 'injustice'.

qa.q: Read: 'The panchayat gave its decision.' What is a 'decision'?
qa.e: A decision is what you choose after thinking about something.

qa.q: Which prefix makes the opposite of 'agree'?
qa.e: dis + agree = disagree.

qa.q: Read: 'The two farmers had a quarrel.' What is a 'quarrel'?
qa.e: A quarrel is when people argue angrily.

qa.q: Which sentence uses speech marks correctly?
qa.a: The Sarpanch said, "Let the calf choose."
qa.e: Only her exact words are inside the speech marks, and they start with a capital.

qa.q: Read: Harish asked, "Is the calf mine?" What were Harish's exact words?
qa.e: The words inside the speech marks are exactly what he said.

qa.q: Choose: "Where is my calf?" ___ Anil.
qa.e: Anil is asking a question, so 'asked' fits best.

qa.q: What do speech marks show?
qa.e: Speech marks hold the words a person actually spoke.

qa.q: In 'The Sarpanch said, "let the calf choose."', what is wrong?
qa.a: 'let' should begin with a capital L
qa.e: The first spoken word always begins with a capital letter.

qa.q: Which word fits: "The calf is mine," ___ Anil, after the Sarpanch asked him.
qa.e: He is answering the Sarpanch, so 'replied' fits.

qa.q: Where does the question mark go in: Anil asked, "Is this your calf"
qa.e: It goes inside: Anil asked, "Is this your calf?"

qa.q: Choose the right punctuation: Anil said ___ "Thank you."
qa.e: A comma comes after 'said' and before the speech marks.

qa.q: Read: 'I watch the baker knead the bread.' What is the baker doing?
qa.e: The line says the baker kneads the bread.

qa.q: Read: 'The postman cycles down our street.' Who cycles down the street?
qa.e: The line names the postman.

qa.q: Read: 'The farmer sows the seeds of wheat.' What does the farmer sow?
qa.e: The farmer sows wheat seeds.

qa.q: Read: 'The farmer sows the seeds of wheat, / The postman cycles down our street.' Which word rhymes with 'wheat'?
qa.e: 'Wheat' and 'street' end with the same sound.

qa.q: Read: 'I wonder, when I'm grown and tall, / Which one I'll be, or maybe all!' What is the child wondering?
qa.a: Which work they will do when they grow up
qa.e: The child wonders which of these jobs they will choose one day.

qa.q: Read: 'I watch the baker knead the bread.' What does 'knead' mean?
qa.a: To press and fold dough with the hands
qa.e: Knead means to press and fold dough. It sounds like 'need', but the meaning is different.

qa.q: Which word rhymes with 'tall' in the poem?
qa.e: 'Tall' and 'all' end with the same '-all' sound.

qa.q: What is the poem mainly about?
qa.a: The work people do and a child's dreams
qa.e: It describes workers and ends with the child wondering about the future.

qa.q: What is a person who teaches called?
qa.e: teach + er = teacher.

qa.q: What is a person who sails a ship called?
qa.e: Sail takes the ending -or: sailor.

qa.q: What is a person who plays music called?
qa.e: Music takes the ending -ian: musician.

qa.q: What do we call a person who studies science?
qa.e: Science becomes scientist.

qa.q: Who fixes the wires, switches and fans in a house?
qa.e: An electrician works with electric wiring.

qa.q: What is a person who acts in plays or films called?
qa.e: act + or = actor.

qa.q: Who mends shoes?
qa.e: A cobbler mends and makes shoes. A carpenter works with wood.

qa.q: What does 'occupation' mean?
qa.a: The work a person does to earn a living
qa.e: Your occupation is your job or work.

qa.q: What is the future form of 'I paint'?
qa.e: Future: will + base verb. So 'I will paint'.

qa.q: Choose: 'When I grow up, I ___ a pilot.'
qa.e: 'When I grow up' points to the future, so we use 'will become'.

qa.q: Which sentence is about the future?
qa.a: Riya will visit the museum tomorrow.
qa.e: 'Will visit' and 'tomorrow' show the future.

qa.q: What is the short form of 'will not'?
qa.e: 'Will not' becomes 'won't', with the apostrophe between n and t.

qa.q: Choose: 'Next week, we ___ trees in the school garden.'
qa.e: 'Next week' is in the future, so we use 'will plant'.

qa.q: Which future-tense sentence is correct?
qa.a: She will dance at the function.
qa.e: After 'will' we always use the base verb: dance.

qa.q: Read: 'I am going to learn the tabla.' What does this sentence show?
qa.e: 'Going to' shows a plan for the future.

qa.q: Which sentence tells about a dream for the future?
qa.a: I want to be a scientist when I grow up.
qa.e: It tells what the speaker wishes to become in the future.

qa.q: Read: 'Zoya's family makes glass bangles in Firozabad.' Where does Zoya's family make bangles?
qa.e: The line names Firozabad, a city famous for glass bangles.

qa.q: Read: 'Glass is melted in a very hot furnace. Her uncle shapes the soft, glowing glass into long coils. The coils are cut into rings.' What is done to the glass first?
qa.a: It is melted in a very hot furnace
qa.e: The glass must be melted and made soft before it can be shaped.

qa.q: Read: 'Her uncle shapes the soft, glowing glass into long coils.' What shape does the glass take first?
qa.e: The uncle shapes the glass into long coils.

qa.q: Read: 'The ends of each ring are joined with a small flame.' How are the ends of each ring joined?
qa.e: Heat softens the glass so the ends can join.

qa.q: Read: 'Then Zoya's mother paints tiny flowers on them.' What does Zoya's mother do?
qa.a: She paints tiny flowers on the bangles
qa.e: The line says she paints tiny flowers on them.

qa.q: Read: ''Each bangle carries the work of many hands,' she says proudly.' What does she mean?
qa.a: Many people work to make one bangle
qa.e: Each step is done by a skilled person, so many people help make each bangle.

qa.q: Read: 'Glass is melted in a very hot furnace, so Zoya watches from a safe distance.' Why does Zoya stay away?
qa.e: A furnace hot enough to melt glass is dangerous, so children stay at a safe distance.

qa.q: Firozabad, the city of glass bangles, is in which state?
qa.e: Firozabad is in Uttar Pradesh. It is famous for glass bangles.

qa.q: What is an artisan?
qa.a: A skilled worker who makes things by hand
qa.e: Artisans use skill and their hands to make useful and beautiful things.

qa.q: A potter works with ___.
qa.e: Potters shape clay into pots, diyas and cups.

qa.q: What does a weaver make?
qa.e: A weaver weaves threads together on a loom to make cloth.

qa.q: A blacksmith works with ___.
qa.e: A blacksmith heats and hammers iron to make tools.

qa.q: What does a goldsmith make?
qa.e: A goldsmith makes ornaments from gold.

qa.q: Madhubani paintings are a famous art from which state?
qa.e: Madhubani painting comes from the Mithila region of Bihar.

qa.q: Channapatna in Karnataka is famous for ___.
qa.e: Channapatna is known for its colourful wooden toys.

qa.q: Why should we value handmade things?
qa.a: They take skill, time and hard work
qa.e: Each handmade item is the result of an artisan's skill and patience.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'glass'?
qa.e: 'Glass' ends in ss, so we add -es: glasses.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'box'?
qa.e: 'Box' ends in x, so we add -es.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'city'?
qa.e: City ends in a consonant + y, so change y to i and add -es.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'toy'?
qa.e: 'Toy' ends in a vowel + y, so we just add -s.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'knife'?
qa.e: 'Knife' changes f to v and adds -es: knives.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'child'?
qa.e: 'Child' changes completely: children. It already means many, so never add another -s.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'sheep'?
qa.e: 'Sheep' stays the same: one sheep, ten sheep.

qa.q: Which sentence uses the plural correctly?
qa.a: The women are painting the bangles.
qa.e: The plural of 'woman' is 'women', and it goes with 'are'.
